hints: Notice particle X is at zero displacement on the displacement-distance graph at $t=0$, on a section with positive slope where the curve is rising toward $\lambda$.
For a wave travelling to the right, the particle velocity is opposite in sign to the slope $dy/dx$, so a positive slope means the particle is moving in the negative displacement direction.
A displacement-time graph for X must therefore start at $0$ at $t=0$ and go negative first, then oscillate with period $T$.
walkthrough: Read the distance graph at $t=0$: displacement is plotted against distance up to wavelength $\lambda$, the wave travels to the right, and particle X is at $y=0$ just before $\lambda$.
Find the slope at X: the curve comes up from the trough and continues up toward the next crest, so $dy/dx$ is positive at X.
Use the progressive-wave rule for motion to the right: particle velocity $dy/dt = -v \times dy/dx$, where $v$ is wave speed. Positive slope gives negative $dy/dt$.
So at $t=0$ particle X has displacement $0$ and velocity in the negative direction - it is moving down through equilibrium.
In time, X must execute simple harmonic motion with period $T$: $0$ going negative, to negative trough, back to $0$, to positive crest, back to $0$ at $t=T$.
Only the graph that starts at $0$ and goes downward first shows this history. This is option C.

A.explanation: Starts at zero and moves positive first, which would mean particle X moves up at $t=0$, opposite to its true downward motion.

B.explanation: Starts at maximum positive displacement, which describes the particle at distance $0$, not particle X which is at zero displacement at $t=0$.

C.explanation: Starts at zero and moves negative first, matching particle X at equilibrium moving down as the wave advances to the right.

D.explanation: Starts at negative displacement at $t=0$, but particle X is at zero displacement on the distance graph at $t=0$.
